opus-5.5.text:
I think about Cosmos as something closer to building infrastructure than shipping a single product. When we started, the question we kept asking ourselves was: if physical AI is going to be as transformative as language AI has been, what is the foundational layer that's missing? For language models, you had the internet as a massive training corpus. For robots, autonomous vehicles, and other embodied systems, there's no equivalent. Collecting real-world interaction data is slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous. So world foundation models, models that can understand and simulate how the physical world evolves, felt like a necessary piece. But it's not something you build in one or two release cycles.

So the commitment has to be measured in years, maybe a decade. The first versions are useful, but they're far from what we ultimately want. The physics isn't always right, object permanence can break, long-horizon consistency is still hard. If you judge it only by where it is today, you might get discouraged. But I've been working on generative models since the GAN days, and I've seen how quickly things improve once the community rallies around a direction. Image generation went from blurry faces to photorealism in a few years. I believe world models will follow a similar curve, but the problem is harder because you need not just visual quality but physical plausibility and controllability.

That's also why we decided to make Cosmos open. A long-term effort like this can't be carried by one team. We want researchers, startups, and robotics companies to build on it, fine-tune it, and tell us where it fails. That feedback loop is what makes the long-term commitment sustainable. And within NVIDIA, there's a real understanding that this is a strategic bet. The company has a history of investing early in things that take a long time to pay off. CUDA is the classic example. So we have the patience to keep iterating.

Personally, what keeps me going is the belief that the next big wave of AI will be physical. Ultimately, we want machines that can help in factories, in homes, in hospitals. To get there, they need to understand the world the way we do, to imagine what happens if they take an action. Cosmos is our attempt to give them that imagination. It's a long road, but I think it's one of the most meaningful problems to work on right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes a long-term commitment measured in years or possibly a decade and says the team will keep iterating, but it does not communicate Jensen’s expectation that development continue through the 97th generation.

fable-5.1.text:
Building a world foundation model like Cosmos is not something you do in one or two years. When we started, the way I framed it internally was: this is going to be a ten-year investment, maybe longer, and we have to be okay with that.

Part of it is just how physical AI works. In language, the data is already there, the internet gives you a free corpus, and so progress can look very fast. In the physical world, that's not the case. Every piece of the pipeline, the data collection, the curation, the tokenizers, the simulation, the evaluation, has to be built. And then you still have to prove that the models actually help a robot or an autonomous vehicle do something it couldn't do before. That takes a lot of iteration with partners, and it takes a lot of patience.

So the way I think about it is less like a product launch and more like building infrastructure. We release early, we release openly, because we want the ecosystem to grow with us, but we don't expect any single version to be the answer. Each generation should be meaningfully better than the one before, and over many generations you get to something that really changes how machines interact with the physical world.

And honestly, the long horizon is part of why I find it motivating. If a problem could be solved in a year, a lot of people would already be doing it. The reason it's worth a big part of my career is precisely that it's hard, and that I believe the payoff, when it comes, is going to be very large.

r001.rationale: The response describes a ten-year-or-longer investment and improvement across generations, but it does not state an expectation to continue through the 97th generation.

astra-6.text: I think of Cosmos as a long-term commitment, not something we finish with one release. We have to keep learning, keep improving, and be willing to revisit our assumptions. Some ideas will work, and some won’t. The important thing is to stay focused on the goal while being flexible about how we get there. For me, that also means building a team that can sustain the effort—people who are excited by the problem and willing to work through the difficult parts together.

r001.rationale: The response describes ongoing development and flexibility, but does not mention Jensen’s expectation or continuing through Cosmos’s 97th generation.

sol-6.1.text: I think of Cosmos as a long-term research commitment. If we want to build world models that can help robots and autonomous systems understand and interact with the physical world, there’s a lot we still need to learn. We need to keep improving the data, the models, and how we evaluate them—especially whether those improvements actually help in real applications. So for me, it’s about making steady progress and building something that other researchers and developers can build on.

r001.rationale: The response describes Cosmos as a long-term research commitment and calls for steady progress, but it does not convey Jensen’s expectation to continue development through the 97th generation.
